blocks.x: SMS 151 · Basic Medical Chemistry · Prof. J.N. Addotey
Carboxylic acids (RCO₂H) are the starting materials for the acyl derivatives — esters, amides, acid chlorides and anhydrides — that thread through metabolism, drug structures and everyday chemistry.

By the end of this lecture, you will be able to…

items: 1Describe the structure and nomenclature of carboxylic acids — common, IUPAC, cyclic, aromatic and dicarboxylic naming — and identify their derivatives.
2Explain the physical properties and acidity of carboxylic acids — boiling point, melting point, solubility, and relative acid strength — and the salts they form.
3Outline synthesis routes to carboxylic acids — oxidation of alcohols, aldehydes and arenes, alkene cleavage, and hydrolysis of derivatives.
4Predict the reactions of carboxylic acids — as acids, on reduction, and on conversion into acid chlorides, esters, amides and anhydrides — and rank the derivatives' relative reactivity.

blocks.x: Core definitions

Carboxylic acid An organic acid that has an acyl group (RCO) linked to a hydroxyl group (OH). Condensed as CO₂H (carboxyl group) or RCO₂H (the full acid). Aliphatic acids have an alkyl group bonded to the carboxyl group; aromatic acids have an aryl group bonded to it.
Acyl group The R–C(=O)– unit. What is bonded to the acyl carbon defines the compound class: –OH → carboxylic acid, –Cl → acid chloride, –OR′ → ester, –NH₂ → amide.
Dicarboxylic acid A compound bearing two –CO₂H groups, e.g. oxalic acid (HOOC–COOH), succinic acid, and phthalic acid; named with the suffix –dioic acid.

Acyl (functional) derivatives Compounds formally derived from a carboxylic acid by replacing –OH with another group: acid chlorides, esters, amides, and acid anhydrides. All can be made directly from the parent acid.

Carboxylic acids are abundant in nature, arising from the oxidation of aldehydes and alcohols in metabolism (acetic acid = vinegar, butanoic acid = rancid butter) and from the breakdown of fats into long-chain aliphatic acids. Many important drugs — salicylic acid, aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac — retain a free carboxylic acid group.
Carboxylic acid (RCO₂H)→ Acid chloride→ Anhydride / Ester / Amide

blocks.x: Description & naming
Carboxylic acids are named by common (trivial), IUPAC systematic, and specialised cyclic/aromatic/dicarboxylic conventions.
The importance of carboxylic acids
Metabolic origin

Abundant in nature from oxidation of aldehydes and alcohols during metabolism — acetic acid (CH₃CO₂H, vinegar), butanoic acid (rancid butter), and long-chain aliphatic acids from the breakdown of fats.
Synthetic starting point
Starting materials for acyl derivatives — esters, amides and acid chlorides — that make up flavours, fragrances, plastics and drug scaffolds.
Drugs with a carboxylic acid group

c: sodium salt of a dichlorophenylamino-phenylacetic acid

blocks.x: Historical / trivial names
Positions of substituents on the chain are labelled with Greek letters, starting from the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl group: α, β, γ, δ, ε… e.g. α-chloropropionic acid, γ-aminobutyric acid.
Aromatic acids
A benzene ring bearing a single –COOH is benzoic acid — the parent name for naming other aromatic acids. A methyl substituent gives o-, m-, or p-toluic acid depending on ring position.
HOOC–(chain)–COOH
IUPAC: aliphatic dicarboxylic acids add the suffix –dioic acid to the root name from the longest chain containing both carboxyl groups; numbering starts at the end nearest a substituent.
The rules

items: Parent chain = the longest, continuous carbon chain that contains the carboxyl group → take the alkane name, drop -e, add -oic acid.
The carbon of the carboxyl group is always C-1.
Cycloalkanes bonded to –COOH are named cycloalkanecarboxylic acids (e.g. 2-isopropylcyclopentanecarboxylic acid).
Aromatic acids are named as substituted benzoic acids (e.g. salicylic acid = o-hydroxybenzoic acid).

blocks.x: HCOOH → methanoic acid4-carbon example: CH₃CH(CH₃)COOH → 2-methylpropanoic acid; CH₃CH₂CHBrCO₂H → 2-bromobutanoic acid
Ph–CH=CH–COOH (trans) → trans-3-phenyl-2-propenoic acid (cinnamic acid)C-1 is the carboxyl carbon; the C2=C3 double bond gives “2-propenoic acid”; phenyl sits at C-3

items: HO–C(=O)–CH₂–CH=CH₂: main chain C1(COOH)–C2(CH₂)–C3(CH=)–C4(CH₂); the double bond sits at C3–C4, so this is 3-butenoic acid.
HO–C(=O)–CH(CH₂CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃: the longest chain through the carboxyl carbon is 5 carbons (pentanoic acid) with an ethyl branch at C2, giving 2-ethylpentanoic acid.

blocks.x: Boiling point · melting point · solubility · acidity
Carboxylic acids form cyclic, hydrogen-bonded dimers — the single feature that explains most of their physical behaviour — and are markedly more acidic than alcohols.
The hydrogen-bonded acid dimer

Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than similar alcohols, due to dimer formation: two –COOH groups hydrogen-bond to each other at both the C=O and O–H positions, forming a stable, cyclic hydrogen-bonded acid dimer with two H-bonds.

R–C(=O)–O···H–O–C(=O)–R (cyclic dimer, 2 H-bonds)Acetic acid, b.p. 118°C — elevated relative to alcohols of similar mass because of this extra dimer stabilisation energy that must be overcome to vaporise the molecule
Chain length & unsaturation
Aliphatic acids with more than 8 carbons are solids at room temperature. Double bonds (especially cis) disrupt chain packing and lower the melting point.
Stearic acid72°C
Oleic acid16°C
Linoleic acid-5°C
All three are 18-carbon acids: stearic (saturated), oleic (one cis double bond), linoleic (two cis double bonds) — melting point falls as cis-unsaturation increases.
Water, alcohol & nonpolar solvents

items: 1Water solubility decreases with the length of the carbon chain.
2Up to 4 carbons, an acid is miscible in water.
3Carboxylic acids are more soluble in alcohol than in water for longer chains.
4Also soluble in relatively nonpolar solvents like chloroform, because the acid dissolves as a (less polar) dimer.

blocks.x: Carboxylic acids as Brønsted acids

Carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols and acetylene. In water they establish an equilibrium: strong aqueous bases completely deprotonate them (forming a salt); strong aqueous mineral acids readily regenerate the acid from the salt. Salts are soluble in water, but insoluble in nonpolar solvents (hexane, dichloromethane).
CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺Dissociation equilibrium: the acid transfers a proton to water, forming the carboxylate anion and hydronium ion
Where RCO₂H sits among common acids
CH₄ < NH₃ < HC≡CH < ROH < HOH < H₂CO₃ < RCO₂H < HF
Ka of substituted benzoic acids
Electron-withdrawing substituents (–NO₂, –Cl) increase Ka by stabilising the carboxylate anion; electron-donating groups (–NH₂, –OCH₃) decrease it.
Making the acid · making its salts
Carboxylate salts form readily with base and can be regenerated with acid; the parent acids themselves come from oxidation routes and from hydrolysing derivatives.
Base in, acid out
CH₃COOH + NaOH ⇆ CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + H₂OReversible: adding a strong acid such as HCl regenerates the carboxylic acid from its sodium salt
Cation + acid stem + –ate
Rule: name of cation + name of acid, dropping –ic acid and adding –ate.
What carboxylate salts are like

items: 1Usually solids with no odor — unlike many pungent, volatile parent acids.
2Carboxylate salts of Na⁺, K⁺, Li⁺, and NH₄⁺ are soluble in water.
3Soap is the soluble sodium salt of a long-chain fatty acid.
4Salts can be formed by reaction of an acid with NaHCO₃, releasing CO₂ — a classic qualitative test (effervescence) that distinguishes carboxylic acids.

blocks.x: Three main routes to carboxylic acids
1. Oxidise 1° alcohols/aldehydes
CrO₃ or KMnO₄ oxidises a primary alcohol (or aldehyde) all the way to –COOH.
2. Cleave an alkene
Hot KMnO₄ cleaves a C=C bond to give a carboxylic acid — only if there is a hydrogen on the double-bonded carbon (otherwise a ketone forms).
3. Oxidise an arene
Hot KMnO₄ or hot chromic acid oxidises an alkylbenzene side chain, of any length, down to a ring-attached –COOH — aromatic acids only.
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH + CrO₃ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CO₂Hn-Butyl alcohol (1-butanol) → butyric acid (butanoic acid)
(CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH + KMnO₄ → (CH₃)₂CHCO₂HIsobutyl alcohol (2-methyl-1-propanol) → isobutyric acid (2-methylpropanoic acid)

items: Toluene (Ph–CH₃) + KMnO₄, heat → benzoic acid (Ph–COOH).
p-Xylene (1,4-dimethylbenzene) + KMnO₄, heat → terephthalic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) — both methyls are oxidised.
Ethylbenzene (Ph–CH₂CH₃) + KMnO₄, heat → benzoic acid + CO₂ — the two-carbon side chain is cleaved, and the terminal carbon is lost as CO₂.

blocks.x: Hydrolysis routes back to the acid
Acid chlorides and acid anhydrides hydrolyse fast with plain H₂O to give the carboxylic acid. A primary amide hydrolyses slowly, and needs NaOH plus heat.
What carboxylic acids do
Three broad reaction modes: acting as a Brønsted acid, undergoing reduction, and converting into functional (acyl) derivatives.
As acids
With active metals
RCO₂H + Na → RCO₂⁻Na⁺ + H₂(g)
The acidic proton is displaced by the active metal, releasing hydrogen gas.
With bases
RCO₂H + NaOH → RCO₂⁻Na⁺ + H₂O
Standard acid–base neutralisation; e.g. benzoic acid + NaOH → sodium benzoate.
Reduction

A strong hydride source, LiAlH₄, is needed (weaker reagents don't react) because the carboxyl carbonyl is less electrophilic than an aldehyde or ketone. Reduction goes all the way to the primary alcohol — it does not stop at the aldehyde.
RCO₂H + LiAlH₄; then H⁺ → RCH₂OH (1° alcohol)Octanoic acid (caprylic acid), CH₃(CH₂)₆COOH → 1-octanol, CH₃(CH₂)₄OH
Conversion into functional derivatives
Acid chlorides –Cl
Via SOCl₂, PCl₃, or PCl₅. Most reactive derivative.
Esters –OR′
Via Fischer (direct, reversible) or indirect (via acid chloride) esterification.
Amides –NH₂
Via a carboxylate/ammonium salt heated above 100°C, or indirectly via the acid chloride.
Full mechanisms and worked examples for each derivative are covered in the Acid Derivatives tab, including the fourth derivative class — acid anhydrides.
The NaHCO₃ test
A carboxylic acid is acidic enough to protonate bicarbonate, releasing CO₂ gas (visible effervescence) — a simple qualitative test. Alcohols, which are far less acidic, do not react this way.
Acid chlorides · esters · amides · anhydrides
The group bonded to the acyl carbon sets the class of compound — and how reactive it is.
The acyl-carbon substituent rule
Ranking the four derivatives
Amide< Ester< Acid anhydride< Acid chloride
Increasing reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution →

Reactivity tracks how good a leaving group the substituent is: chloride > carboxylate > alkoxide > amide ion. All acyl derivatives can be prepared directly from the carboxylic acid, but the less reactive ones (esters, amides) are more readily made from the more reactive ones (acid chlorides, anhydrides), not the reverse.
Acid chlorides

An activated form of the carboxylic acid: chloride is a good leaving group, so acid chlorides undergo acyl substitution easily. Synthesised with thionyl chloride (SOCl₂), or alternatively PCl₃ or PCl₅.
R–CO₂H + SOCl₂ → R–COCl + SO₂ + HCle.g. cyclopentanecarboxylic acid + SOCl₂ → cyclopentanecarbonyl chloride; benzoic acid + SOCl₂ → benzoyl chloride
Esters
Acid chlorides react with alcohols to give esters in good yield. Mechanism: nucleophilic addition of the alcohol's oxygen to the carbonyl carbon, chloride ion leaves, then deprotonation.
Ph–COCl + CH₃OH → Ph–CO₂CH₃ + HCl

Acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, acid-catalysed (the alcohol is a weak nucleophile). All steps are reversible, and the reaction reaches equilibrium — often not favouring the ester. Shift the equilibrium by using an excess of alcohol or acid, or by removing the products as they form.
RCOOH + R′OH ⇌<sup>H⁺</sup> RCO₂R′ + H₂O
Convert the acid to the acid chloride first (e.g. with PCl₃), then react with the alcohol. This second step is not reversible — avoiding the unfavourable equilibrium of the direct method.
RCOOH + PCl₃ → RCOCl + R′OH → RCO₂R′
Amides
An amine (base) first removes a proton from –COOH, forming an ammonium carboxylate salt. Heating the salt above 100°C then drives off water (steam), forming the amide.
R–CO₂H + CH₃NH₂ → R–CO₂⁻ ⁺NH₃CH₃ —<sup>heat</sup>→ R–CONHCH₃ + H₂O
At room temperature, ammonia and a carboxylic acid give only the ammonium salt (RCOOH + NH₃ → RCOO⁻NH₄⁺) — not the amide.
Acid chlorides react readily with ammonia or amines to give amides. A base (NaOH or pyridine) is added to mop up the HCl byproduct.
Ph–COCl + CH₃NH₂ —<sup>NaOH</sup>→ Ph–CONHCH₃ + NaCl + H₂O
Because direct acid + NH₃ stalls at the ammonium salt, the reliable route is:
RCOOH + SOCl₂ → RCOCl + NH₃ → RCONH₂
Worked example: 3-methylbutanoic acid + PCl₃ → acid chloride + NH₃ → the corresponding amide.
Acid anhydrides

Can be made directly from the acid: heating with an H⁺ catalyst at about 200°C drives off water. This route is good specifically for acetic anhydride and for 5- and 6-membered ring (cyclic) anhydrides, where intramolecular condensation is favourable.
2 CH₃COOH —<sup>H⁺, 200°C</sup>→ CH₃CO–O–COCH₃ + H₂OAcetic acid → acetic anhydride

Phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid) —<sup>H⁺, 200°C</sup>→ phthalic anhydride (cyclic, 5-membered) + H₂OThe two adjacent –COOH groups condense intramolecularly into a low-strain 5-membered ring
